beats.say: Long ago, there were no fridges. So in eighteen thirty three, a ship carried a mountain of ice all the way from America to Calcutta.
The trip took four months. And more than half of the ice was still ice when it arrived!
So how does a fridge keep your food cold? Let's find out.
First, try this. Wet your hand, and blow on it. Feels cold, right?
When water dries up, it takes heat away with it. That is the whole secret of a fridge.
In seventeen fifty five, a teacher in Scotland, William Cullen, made ice just by letting a liquid dry up really fast.
In eighteen thirty four, Jacob Perkins patented a machine that did this again and again, in a loop. That's the grandfather of your fridge.
Inside your fridge, a special liquid runs through thin pipes. It dries up into a gas, and grabs the heat from your food.
Then a pump squeezes the gas. Squeezing makes it hot.
At the back, the hot gas gives its heat to your room, and turns back into liquid. Round and round it goes.
Here's the funny part. A fridge doesn't make cold. It carries heat out of the box, like a bucket carrying water out of a boat.
That's why the back of your fridge feels warm!
Even Albert Einstein helped invent a fridge. The nineteen thirty patent had no squeezing pump at all.
In India, Godrej says it made the first Indian fridge in nineteen fifty eight. Today, about thirty eight out of every hundred homes have one.
